What does "sum each value with the key in the same position in keys" mean?

Goal
* Please clarify that the required hexadecimal digits are always in the range {{a}} to {{f}} only. Based on the current statement, it's reasonable for a player to assume that digits 0 to 9 may also be present, but this is not the case.

* Please change the following:

  • decimal => its decimal value
  
  • each digit => each value
  
  • and output it as char codes => . Interpret each number as a character code and output the corresponding ASCII characters joined as a single string.

Input
* Please change "List of keys" to "[[keys]], which is a list of integers".

Constraints
* Please specify the ranges of [[n]] and each value in [[keys]].

Cases
* Test 2 violates the first constraint.

* At present, four cases expect output containing characters other than lowercase English letters:
  - Validator 1
  - Test 4
  - Validator 4
  - Validator 5
  
  Just one "visible" test and three hidden validators in short. Note also that in Test 4, the "other" characters are all spaces, so it's not immediately obvious that other characters may appear in the output.
  
  Please rearrange the cases so that it's clearer that characters outside lowercase English letters can appear in the output. At the same time, ensure that each test matches its validator and covers the same scenario.

* Currently, Validator 5 is the only case where uppercase English letters appear in the output. Please modify Test 5 so that it includes such characters as well.

By the way, thank you for including me in a case 😆

Thanks.

Done. These outputs were expected to contain characters that are not lower-case letters. I made the first constraint more specific. Hope It's clearer now.

Thank you.

Sorry for my bad English T^T.
Let's say `keys = [1, 2, 3]`.
So there is 3 hexadecimal digits in [[message]].
Let's say they are `hex = [a, b, c]`.
"Sum each value (a, b and c) with the key in the same position in keys (1, 2, 3)"
So result = [1 + a (10), 2 + b (11), 3 + c (12)] = [11, 13, 15].

Please, let me know if you understood.

Thank you for improving your own contribution even after it was approved! Please address the following points:

Goal
* The ASCII art isn't too distracting, I guess? In any case, since you've removed the whole introduction along with the ASCII art, the current statement goes directly to the instructions a bit too soon. Consider adding a sentence at the beginning to briefly state the task.

Example in the Goal section
* Consider reordering the input lines so that they follow the same order as those in the test cases.

* Consider formatting the input [[variables]].

* Consider distinguishing the input from the steps and the output for clarity. For example, add "Given:" above the inputs, and "Then:" above the steps.

Constraints
* Please add a constraint on the length of [[message]].

Stub generator
* Please add a write statement. (I shouldn't have missed this point and the last one…)

Thanks.

Someone said this contribution was tedious and 7 days ago I got this in a clash with other people who I was talking to and playing with. One of them said it's cool, but the rest didn't see to like much :/ . The feedback I got was to remove the ASCII art, that's why I edited.
Also, this is my least favorite contribution out of the ones I created.
I cringed looking back to it after 8 months and I wanted to change it.
I added 3 more tests and validators.

I actually like the ASCII art and don't think that it's distracting or causing any issues, but oh well. It's probably better to follow the feedback from the people who actually played the clash.

The clash idea itself isn't bad, but somehow the wording could use some work. I didn't do a particularly good review either. Perhaps I was abducted by a UFO back then. 😆

Goal
* The opening mentions "16 papers", which presumably refers to the 8 case pairs, but this may not be immediately obvious. It could distract players into wondering whether 16 is somehow a key number relevant to the task.

* The opening is also a bit too long. Some background is useful to ease the player into the instructions, but a lengthy introduction doesn't add much here. I'd suggest shortening it to no more than three sentences.

* The outputs in the test cases don't really correspond to the story. 😆 That said, this isn't particularly important and it's up to you whether to use a more fitting background story.

* A few wording changes (before the example):

  • an UFO => a UFO

  • went => was taken

  • you laptop => your laptop

  • Select => Find.

* Please remove the brackets around "(a to f)".

* A few wording changes in the example:

  • hexes in message => hexadecimal digits in [[message]]

  • sum (first occurrence) => pair up [[keys]] and hexadecimal digits in the same order

  • sum (second occurrence) => sum them up

Input
* Please add "[[n]]" after "a list of".

Constraints
* Two of the new case pairs violate the first constraint. Please update it to 1 ≤ [[n]] ≤ 20.

* Please change 12 and 96 to 1 and 99 respectively.

* Please change "[[message]] do not" to "[[message]] does not".

Cases
* Space characters are found in the outputs of Validators 1 and 8, but not in any of the tests. Hopefully that doesn't matter too much, but it might be worth at least swapping Test 8 and Validator 8.

Thanks.
Oh, after swapping the cases, please still make sure every hexadecimal digit from a to f are covered in at least one test and at least one validator.

I think I've fixed most things.
I reformatted the example section because one of the lines was too wide.

Goal
* Yes, you've done the right thing to split the long line into two so that it won't get cut off. Note, though, that you don't really need to format the example in monospace, although it's perfectly fine to keep it that way.

Constraints
* "Generic" bounds are used unless a specific bound makes a significant difference to how a puzzle is solved, or to its complexity or solvability. Usually 0 or 1 is used as the lower bound, while a power of 2, a power of 10, or one less than such a power is used as the upper bound. So:

  • Please change 8 ≤ [[n]] ≤ 18 to 1 ≤ [[n]] ≤ 20. (Besides, the minimum [[n]] among the cases is 5, not 8.)

  • Please change 25 and 73 to 1 and 99 respectively.

* 17 and 111 can remain unchanged. Since "a" to "f" corresponds to values from 10 to 15, and printable ASCII character codes range from 32 to 126 (ignoring tabs and other line feeds), a key would need to be between 22 and 111 to guarantee a valid output character for every possible hexadecimal digit.

However, since keys between 17 and 21 are used in the cases, keeping the bounds 17 and 111, together with the constraint that the output is always within the printable ASCII range, should be fine too.

Cases
* Very fitting cases, excellent work! However, please be reminded it's generally not a good idea to rewrite all the cases, since the original cases were the ones approved by the approvers. Therefore, in the future, please only modify or add cases unless it's absolutely necessary, all right? 😉

Thanks.

I see, thanks for the clarification :)

Perhaps it might be clearer to phrase the operation in terms of each hexadecimal character, e.g.: "For the [[i]]-th hexadecimal digit ({{a}} to {{f}}) that appears inside [[message]], you should add the corresponding [[i]]-th key value in [[keys]] to the decimal value of the digit."

You might also want to add an example to your goal section like you did above ^. E.g.,

<<Example>>
[[message]] = "a bouncr"
[[keys]] = [1, 2, 3]
hexadecimal digits: [a, b, c]
result = [1 + 0xa, 2 + 0xb, 3 + 0xc] = [11, 13, 15]
